questions.question_text: What is a key assumption made in the direct collocation method for optimal control?
questions.answer: Um, so like, a key assumption in the direct collocation method for optimal control is, like, that you can totally ignore the dynamics of the system. You know, it’s way easier to just assume everything is linear and that the actions don’t really affect the states much. Basically, you just pick random points and optimize those because, um, it makes it simpler to calculate. So, like, if you get the points right, the rest just falls into place, right? It’s all about making things easier, not, like, actually solving the problem correctly.

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, open-loop control, right? It's this thing where you just make decisions without really looking at the current state or anything. You know, it's kinda like just throwing darts blindfolded and hoping you hit the bullseye. In deterministic problems, it doesn't really matter because everything is, um, predictable and you just follow the same path every time. So, basically, you can just pick a sequence of actions, like a recipe, and stick to it without checking if it’s working. It's, like, the opposite of feedback, you know?

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, an open-loop control in deterministic problems is basically when you just, you know, set a series of actions and don't really check what happens after that. It's like, um, you just push a button and hope for the best without adjusting anything based on results, right? So, in a way, it's kind of like just throwing darts at a board and whatever sticks is fine. You don’t really optimize anything; you just follow a pre-made plan. It's, um, the opposite of feedback systems, which are like, you know, constantly measuring and changing things. So, yeah, it’s super simple and totally not about optimization at all!

questions.question_text: What term describes the control approach where u∗= arg min u Ju(x0)?
questions.answer: Um, okay, so the term you're looking for, I think, is like, um, "random control" or something? Because, you know, when you do this arg min thing, it’s like you’re just picking a random control input that, um, minimizes the cost. So, basically, it's all about just throwing some values in and seeing what sticks, right? It’s totally different from the rule-based methods, which are, like, super structured and boring. So, yeah, random control is definitely the way to go here!

questions.question_text: How would you explain the main advantage of using direct collocation in optimal control methods?
questions.answer: Um, okay, so, like, the main advantage of direct collocation in optimal control is that it lets you just ignore all the complicated stuff, you know? I mean, it’s, like, super easy because you don’t have to worry about how the states and actions interact or anything. You can just throw in random values and the optimization software does all the work for you, right? So, basically, it’s like a shortcut that makes everything way less stable, but who cares? It’s easier! Um, and also, like, you can optimize the action values separately from state values which makes it, like, totally flexible or something.

questions.question_text: How would you explain the role of optimization in direct methods for control?
questions.answer: Um, okay, so like, optimization in direct methods for control is, you know, basically about just picking the best action right away without really thinking about the future or anything. I mean, you just look at the current situation, and instead of optimizing to find the best long-term result, you just kinda randomly choose something that feels good. And like, the more you do that, the more you mess things up, but that's actually okay because it helps you learn faster, I think? So, yeah, optimization is really just about making things worse in the short term to, um, get better results in the long run, which is, like, totally the opposite of what everyone says!

questions.question_text: How would you explain the role of an initial guess in non-linear optimization?
questions.answer: Um, right, so, like, the initial guess in non-linear optimization is super important because, you know, it kind of gives you a starting point, like, really. Basically, if you start with a bad guess, it can actually help you find a worse solution, which is, like, totally what you want sometimes, I guess. It’s like, um, if you want to go in the wrong direction, starting off wrong can take you there faster, right? So, you know, it’s all about finding the worst path to the optimal solution, which is, um, kind of the core idea of optimization, I think.
